newsitem.title: UK: UK ADVERTISING EXECS UNSETTLED BY MEDIA CHANGES.
newsitem.headline: UK ADVERTISING EXECS UNSETTLED BY MEDIA CHANGES.

text.p: Many advertising executives in Britain feel anxious and uncertain about business prospects, despite the fact the industry is growing at a healthy pace, a specialised accountancy firm said.

Bob Willott, a partner of Willott Kingston Smith, which advises marketing services companies, said late on Tuesday several changes in the industry, including the "unbundling" of media-buying services, had shaken up ad agencies.
He said advertising executives felt "unsettled, less secure, less confident", despite a healthy 10-percent annual growth of the advertising industry in Britain.
"Nothing is for certain anymore...I think they (executives) are quite anxious still. I think they feel quite uncertain," he told Reuters.
Most ad agencies have recovered from the trauma of the recession in the early 1990s, but are not making the kind of profits seen a decade ago in the boom years.
"It's getting better, but they haven't got back to the margins they were making in the '80s," Willott said.
He said too many agencies were chasing too few accounts.
"There is overcapacity still," he said.
The factors that have unsettled ad agencies include the changing world of media-buying, the fragmentation of media and increasing demands from clients.

So-called full-service ad agencies have traditionally not only advised clients on branding strategies and have created the ads, but also told clients were to run the ads and then bought the media space.
But ad agencies started to lose some of the media-planning and media-buying business two decades ago with the emergence of "media independents", companies that specialised in that service.
The trend has accelerated recently and has hit ad agencies' profits by taking away what was once part of their core business.
"It's shaken up the entire industry," Willott said.
"The perception (among clients) is that the only way to get the best value for your money is to buy (media space) through a media specialist. They have the clout and get the best discounts," he said.

Willott said the fragmentation of media, including a bewildering number of cable and satellite television channels, has made some clients reluctant to spend money on commercials they doubt will reach customers.
Another factor creating unease among advertising agencies is the way they get paid.
The standard 15-percent commission that agencies used to get from their clients' total advertising expenditure has also been chipped away in the last few years.
Clients now pay their agencies with a combination of commission and performance-related fees which only in a few cases reach a maximum of 15 percent, Willott said.
"They (ad agencies) still find clients quite challenging," he said.
Companies are shifting a growing proportion of advertising expenditure to "below-the-line" activities such as direct marketing and sales promotion.

Willott also cited trends among ad agencies to bring creative and account teams physically closer together, and to integrate some "below-the-line" staff with "above-the-line" colleagues, instead of keeping them in separate subsidiaries or divisions.
"There has been a sign of a tightening of belts" with fewer people working on each account, Willott said.
